Who We Are

About FarmFix Uganda Ltd

"Fixing Agriculture with Purpose" — a Ugandan agricultural consultancy built on field experience, rigorous research, and genuine commitment to community impact.

Our Story

Built from the field, not the boardroom.

FarmFix Uganda Ltd was established with a clear conviction: that practical, expert agricultural support should be within reach of every farmer, organisation, and community that needs it. We are a Ugandan agricultural consultancy working across the full spectrum of farm management, advisory services, research, project implementation, and community development.

Our team brings together agronomists, social development researchers, project managers, and field practitioners with deep experience across Uganda's diverse farming landscapes — from the fertile highlands of Western Uganda to the semi-arid zones of the north, and in refugee and displacement-affected communities where food security is most fragile.

We have supported smallholder farmers, cooperatives, government programmes, NGOs, and private agribusinesses. Across all of them, our approach is the same: listen carefully, assess honestly, plan realistically, and deliver results that last beyond our involvement.

Field-Level Expertise Since 2010

Kitchen & Demonstration Garden Farming

Good nutrition begins at home.

A well-managed kitchen garden can feed a family of five, reduce food expenditure, and provide fresh vegetables, herbs, and spices year-round — even on a small plot.

We provide training, demonstration visits, and printed guides for farmer groups, schools, NGOs, and settlement communities. Our demo farms have showcased onions, tomatoes, eggplant, passion fruit, beans, soyabeans, hybrid maize, Irish potatoes, and herbs using gravity drip irrigation, vertical conical gardens, and shade-net nurseries.

Humanitarian & Community Projects

Agriculture is often the fastest path back to dignity.

Funding-contingent service: FarmFix implements these programmes when funding is secured through institutional donors, UN agencies, government partners, or INGOs. We welcome conversations with potential funders and implementing partners.

How We Work

The FarmFix Farm Business Cycle

Every successful farm or agricultural project moves through a structured cycle. FarmFix supports clients at every stage — ensuring nothing falls through the cracks.

01
🔍

Diagnosis & Opportunities

A thorough assessment of your farm, context, or community — identifying constraints, strengths, and real opportunities available to you.

02
📐

Planning

Evidence-based planning with seasonal calendars, input plans, financial projections, and work plans — built around what is actually achievable.

03
⚙️

Organising

Labour organisation, input procurement, equipment scheduling, and stakeholder coordination — the logistics that make implementation possible.

04
🌾

Producing

On-the-ground implementation with day-to-day supervision, agronomic guidance, and real-time problem-solving across the growing season.

05
📊

Monitoring

Tracking against plans with regular field visits, data collection, and early warning so issues are caught before they become serious problems.

06
🏪

Marketing

Market linkages, buyer connections, post-harvest handling, and value chain support to protect your income after harvest.

07
📈

Evaluation

What worked, what didn't, what changed — and what to do differently next season. Honest evaluation that improves performance cycle after cycle.

The cycle never truly ends. Evaluation feeds back into better diagnosis and stronger production — creating a continuous improvement loop that builds farm resilience and business performance over time.

Our Commitment

Food & Nutrition Security for Every Community

Uganda hosts over 1.5 million refugees — one of the largest refugee populations in Africa. Our research shows over 82% of refugee households in protracted situations remain food insecure. Agriculture is the fastest and most dignified pathway to change that.

The Challenge

Why this work matters

Despite years of humanitarian support, food insecurity among refugee households in Uganda remains alarmingly high. Our peer-reviewed research in Rhino Camp documented the scope of this crisis — and what can be done about it.

1.5M+
Refugees in Uganda needing food security support
82%
Of refugee households in protracted crisis are food insecure
50.7%
Are severely food insecure despite long-running interventions

Statistics from: Kamugisha et al. (2024), Journal of Interventional Epidemiology and Public Health

What Our Research Found

Key findings from Rhino Camp, Uganda

Our 2024 peer-reviewed study among 432 South Sudanese refugee households in Rhino Camp Refugee Settlement, Arua District, found that food insecurity is driven by modifiable, addressable factors — not simply the refugee situation itself.

📍

Location Within the Settlement

Households in zones with poor soils and low rainfall were significantly more food insecure — highlighting the need for zone-specific agricultural strategies.

🎓

Education Level

Household heads with formal education were nearly 3x more likely to be food secure — largely through employment opportunities with humanitarian organisations.

💰

Monthly Income

Households earning USD 15–45/month were twice as likely to be food secure, underscoring the importance of income diversification beyond farming.

🧒

Adolescent-Headed Households

New households formed by adolescents — often not on initial humanitarian aid plans — were the most food insecure group and the most overlooked.

Research & Publications

Our Research Informs Our Practice

FarmFix's work is grounded in credible, peer-reviewed research. We publish findings on food security, agricultural development, and community livelihoods — and use that evidence to design programmes that actually improve lives.

Published Research

Peer-Reviewed Publications

2024
Research

Prevalence of Food Insecurity and Associated Factors among Refugee Households in Rhino Camp Refugee Settlement, Arua District, Uganda

Kamugisha F., Komakech H., Nakanwagi Kisakye A., Bukenya J.
Journal of Interventional Epidemiology and Public Health (JIEPH), Vol. 7, Issue 1, March 2024. DOI: 10.37432/jieph.2024.7.1.103

This cross-sectional mixed methods study assessed food insecurity prevalence and associated factors among 432 South Sudanese refugee households in a protracted crisis in Rhino Camp, Arua District. Findings revealed that 82.4% of households were food insecure, with 50.7% classified as severely food insecure — higher than the general refugee population estimate of 58%. Key factors associated with food insecurity included geographical location within the settlement (AOR 3.48), age of household heads, education level (AOR 2.68), and monthly income (AOR 2.14). Coping strategies included reducing meal frequency (28%), selling domestic assets (21.7%), and sending household members elsewhere. The study recommends targeted interventions for adolescent-headed households, location-sensitive agricultural approaches, and adult literacy programmes to improve employability and food security.
